A Quiet Revolution, an Uneven Map, and a Pandemic

Four decades of childhood vaccination, told in four beats

Author

Team 15

Published

May 26, 2026

Communication goals. This prototype walks the reader through four beats: (1) the dramatic global rise in childhood vaccination since 1980, (2) the inequalities that persist beneath the global average, (3) the structural — especially economic — drivers of those inequalities, and (4) how the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted decades of progress. Each beat is one chart, one paragraph of narration, and one or two annotations that point directly to the evidence on the chart.

A quiet revolution, 1980–2024

In 1980, fewer than one in five children worldwide was vaccinated against diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis. Today, the figure is more than four in five. That shift — from 20% to 85% in just over four decades — ranks among the largest public-health gains in modern history, yet it rarely shows up in headlines. We open the story there: with the long arc that all of the later complications hang from.

Four of the workhorse vaccines tell the same story. Diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis and polio both crossed the 75% line by 1990 — within a decade of the WHO’s Expanded Programme on Immunization gaining momentum. Hepatitis B took longer because it was added to the routine schedule later, but it has effectively caught up. The global picture, in short, looks like a success.

But “global average” hides a lot

A single global line is reassuring, and misleading. Average coverage in 2024 sits at 85%, but the spread between countries is still enormous: nearly 60 percentage points separate the best- and worst-performing nations. The map below shows where those gaps live. Two African neighbours, Rwanda (98%) and Sudan (39%), sit at opposite ends of the scale in the same year.

The low-coverage band runs through the Sahel, the Horn of Africa, and a handful of conflict-affected states; the high-coverage band covers nearly all of Europe, the Americas, and East Asia. But coverage is not destiny: Rwanda’s 98% rate, achieved at a GDP per capita under $3,500, sits next to wealthy Azerbaijan’s 51% — a result that should be impossible if vaccination were simply a question of money.

Money matters — but it isn’t the whole story

If wealth alone determined vaccination, every country would line up neatly along a single curve. They don’t. Coverage does climb with GDP per capita, but the cloud of dots is wide enough that nearly every income level contains both stars and laggards. The trend is real but loose: a Pearson correlation of roughly r ≈ 0.5 between log-GDP and DTP3 coverage in 2024.

The labelled countries are the story. Rwanda and Bangladesh sit far above the trend line: poor by world-bank measures, but with delivery systems strong enough to reach essentially every infant. On the other side, Azerbaijan and Equatorial Guinea are oil-rich and yet vaccinate at rates more typical of much poorer countries. Money helps, but what really seems to matter is whether a country has a functioning primary-care network to use the money for routine immunization.

A first decline since 1980

Progress is never guaranteed. Between 2019 and 2021, global DTP3 coverage fell from 86% to 82% — the first sustained dip in four decades, driven by COVID-19 lockdowns and the diversion of healthcare workers to pandemic response. By 2024 the world had clawed most of it back, but still sits one percentage point below pre-pandemic peak.

The dip is small in absolute terms but enormous in context: from 1980 through 2019, the line had only ever drifted sideways, never sustained a multi-year fall. Measles coverage has been slowest to recover — and unlike DTP3, measles needs roughly 95% coverage to prevent outbreaks, so the gap matters. The dashboard at the end of this report lets you check whether your country has fully recovered.

What this means — and what to do next

Put together, the four charts tell a single story:

  • Global progress is real. Childhood vaccination coverage has roughly quadrupled in a generation.
  • But the global average hides a 60-point gap between the best and worst performers, and that gap has geographic shape: it concentrates in the Sahel and a handful of conflict states.
  • Wealth predicts coverage on average, but not country-by-country. The countries that punch above their weight tend to share a feature wealth alone doesn’t buy: a working primary-care system.
  • And the system is fragile. A single global shock cost four years of progress, and the recovery isn’t yet complete.

Each beat is built directly from the WHO/UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage (1980–2024) and World Bank GDP per capita data.

Now you explore

The static narrative above takes the same dataset and turns it into four guided moments. The companion dashboard inverts that: it hands the wheel to the reader. Pick any vaccine, drag through any year, click any country to see its full trajectory and compare it to the world average.

→ Run the dashboard: Rscript -e 'shiny::runApp("dashboard")' from the information_visualization/ folder, or open dashboard/app.R in RStudio and click Run App.

TipMethods and caveats
  • Population denominator. Coverage figures describe the share of one-year-olds who received each vaccine in that calendar year — not the share of the whole population.
  • Missing values are kept as gaps, not zeros. For newer vaccines (PCV3, Rotavirus, IPV1) a blank cell typically means the vaccine wasn’t yet on the routine schedule.
  • Recent years are partly estimated. WHO extrapolates from prior reporting when countries don’t report on time, so 2023–2024 numbers should be treated as best-available rather than firm.
  • GDP data starts in 1990. Any cross-data analyses pre-1990 use only the vaccine series.
